title: Growth Equity
summary: Minority stakes in companies that are already working, with little or no leverage — returns come from growth alone.

lesson.body:
[[growth-equity]] sits between [[buyout]] and [[venture-capital]], and it is defined less by company size than by three structural choices.

**Minority stakes.** The fund usually takes 20-40% rather than control. It gets board representation and contractual protections, not the ability to replace management unilaterally.

**Little or no leverage.** The businesses are typically growing fast and often not yet consistently profitable, so they cannot support [[buyout]] debt. The [[commitment|committed capital]] goes into the company to fund expansion rather than to the selling shareholder.

**Proven model, unproven scale.** Unlike venture, the product works and customers pay. Unlike buyout, the question is not efficiency but how large this can get.

That combination has a direct consequence: **remove leverage and remove control, and the return has to come almost entirely from the company growing.**

**The return driver is revenue and earnings growth, plus whatever multiple the market pays at exit.**

Compare that with the [[buyout]] decomposition. Debt paydown contributes nothing, because there is little debt. So of the three buyout value-creation sources, only two remain, and one of them — [[ev-ebitda|multiple]] change — is outside the manager's control.

This makes growth equity a purer bet on the business than buyout is, with both the honesty and the fragility that implies. There is no financial engineering to fall back on. If the company grows into its valuation, the return is good; if growth decelerates, there is nothing to cushion it.

It also means **entry valuation is the dominant risk**. A company growing 40% a year bought at 15x revenue needs years of sustained growth simply to justify the price paid. The same company at 6x has a considerably wider margin for disappointment, with identical operating performance.

The interesting question about a minority stake is: what can you actually do if things go wrong?

The answer is contractual rather than operational. Growth investors negotiate protections into the shareholders' agreement — consent rights over major decisions, board seats, information rights, anti-dilution provisions, liquidation preferences, and rights that force or permit an exit after a period.

**These terms are the substance of the investment**, and this is where a lot of the skill lives. Two funds can buy identical stakes at identical prices with entirely different downside outcomes, because one negotiated a liquidation preference and consent over further fundraising and the other did not.

There is a specific risk worth naming. A minority holder without protections can be **crammed down** in a later round: the company raises new capital at a lower valuation on terms that dilute or subordinate the existing minority holding. The business may even recover, and the earlier investor still does badly. So in growth equity, reading the term sheet is not a legal formality — it is a large part of the analysis, in the same way documentation is for [[distressed-debt]].

lesson.caption: What helps and what hurts
rows: Helps existing holdings reprice upward, hurts new deployment by raising entry valuations.
Strong revenue growth across the economy
The return driver is growth, so a growing economy directly supports it.
Open IPO and strategic acquisition markets
Minority stakes need someone else to buy them. Closed exit markets leave positions stranded.
Long-duration growth assets reprice hardest when discount rates rise — the present value topic applied to a portfolio.
Minority holders without strong protections can be diluted or subordinated in a rescue financing.
With no leverage and no control, growth is the only lever. When it slows, nothing offsets it.

lesson.body:
**Overpaying at entry.** The dominant risk, and the one most visible in hindsight. High-growth businesses bought at high multiples in a competitive market need years of execution just to break even on the price.

**Growth deceleration.** A company growing 50% that slows to 15% is frequently revalued on a completely different multiple — not just a lower number applied to the same framework, but a shift from a growth valuation to a mature one. The compounding of a lower multiple on lower growth is brutal.

**Being crammed down.** As above: a later financing on aggressive terms can subordinate or heavily dilute a minority position that lacked protections.

**No exit.** A minority stake in a private company cannot be sold without a buyer for the whole business, an IPO, or a [[secondaries|secondary]] sale at a discount. Closed exit markets can strand a position for years.

**Rate sensitivity.** Growth companies are long-duration assets — most of their value sits in distant cash flows. That makes them the most rate-sensitive holdings in a private portfolio, for exactly the reasons the discount-factor table demonstrated.

**Ask what the entry valuation was, on what metric.** A revenue multiple in a business with no profits is a different proposition from an EBITDA multiple. Multiples on revenue deserve particular scrutiny, because they are silent about whether the business will ever convert revenue into cash.

**Ask about the protections in the shareholders' agreement.** Consent rights, liquidation preference, anti-dilution, exit rights. This is where minority downside is determined, and a manager who cannot summarise their own protections crisply has not focused on them.

**Ask how many holdings have raised subsequent rounds, and at what valuations.** Up rounds validate; flat and down rounds are the leading indicator of trouble, and they show up well before a mark changes.

**Read growth deceleration as a valuation event, not just a performance one.** A holding whose growth rate has halved may need a multiple reset, and managers are often slow to reflect that in marks.

**Check the exit assumption.** If the underwriting case assumes an IPO, ask what the return looks like on a trade sale instead. Exit route optionality is worth more than the underwriting usually credits.

items: Minority stakes, little leverage, proven model — so the return comes almost entirely from growth plus the exit multiple.
Remove debt paydown from the buyout decomposition and only two sources remain, one of which the manager does not control.
Entry valuation is the dominant risk. Identical operating performance produces very different returns from different entry multiples.
Minority protections in the shareholders' agreement are the substance of the downside, not legal boilerplate.

questions.stem: Which buyout value-creation source is largely unavailable to a growth equity fund?
choices: Operational improvement
Debt paydown
Multiple expansion
Revenue growth
rationales: Growth funds do work with management on operations, though with less authority than a controlling owner.
Correct. Growth companies typically cannot support meaningful debt, so there is no borrowing to repay and no mechanical increase in the equity's share of enterprise value.
Multiple change applies to any equity investment — it is available, though not controllable.
Revenue growth is the strategy's primary return driver, not an unavailable one.
questions.explanation: Removing debt paydown removes both a return source and a cushion. It makes growth equity a purer bet on the business, which is more honest and less forgiving.

questions.stem: Two funds buy identical 25% stakes in the same company at the same price. Why might their downside outcomes differ substantially?
choices: Because one will hold for longer than the other
Because the contractual protections negotiated — consent rights, liquidation preference, anti-dilution — differ
Because minority stakes are valued differently by different managers
Because one fund will use leverage and the other will not
rationales: Holding period matters for IRR but does not explain a difference in downside protection.

Correct. Identical economics with different terms produce different outcomes when things go wrong. Consent over further fundraising, a liquidation preference and anti-dilution provisions all determine what happens in a bad scenario.
Both would eventually be marked against the same realisation. Interim marking differences do not change the outcome.
Growth equity typically uses little leverage at the fund or deal level, and it is not the distinction here.
questions.explanation: This is the central practical point about minority investing: the price tells you the upside and the terms tell you the downside. A manager who negotiates well can lose considerably less on the same failed company.

questions.stem: A holding growing 50% a year decelerates to 15%. Why is the valuation impact typically worse than the growth reduction alone suggests?
choices: Because revenue falls as well as growth
Because the business is often revalued on a different, lower multiple framework — a mature multiple rather than a growth one
Because slower growth triggers debt covenants
Because minority stakes cannot be revalued
rationales: Revenue is still growing at 15%, so it is rising rather than falling. The damage is to the multiple, not the top line.
Correct. A compounding effect: a lower growth rate applied to a materially lower multiple. Businesses do not slide smoothly down a valuation curve — they get re-categorised.
Growth companies typically carry little debt, so covenant breach is not the usual mechanism.
Minority stakes are revalued regularly. The question is whether the manager reflects the re-rating promptly.
questions.explanation: The re-rating is the bigger half of the loss. It is also where private marks tend to lag most visibly, because reflecting a multiple reset requires the manager to concede a change in the character of the business, not just its numbers.

questions.stem: "Growth equity is insulated from interest rates because the companies carry no debt." True or false — and why?
justifications: False — most of a growth company's value sits in distant cash flows, so it is highly sensitive to the discount rate even with no borrowing
False — growth companies actually carry more debt than buyout targets
True — with no debt there is no interest rate exposure
False — because interest rates only affect publicly listed companies
rationales: Correct. Rate exposure comes through two channels: financing cost and discounting. No debt removes the first and does nothing about the second, and for long-duration assets the second is far larger.
Factually wrong — growth companies typically carry considerably less debt than buyout targets.
This conflates the two channels. Being unlevered protects against financing cost, not against the repricing of far-future cash flows.
Discount rates apply to private and public assets alike. Private marks simply reflect it more slowly.
questions.explanation: This is the discount-factor table applied to a portfolio: at a 12% rate, a dollar arriving in twenty years is worth about ten cents. Growth companies hold most of their value in exactly those far-out years, which makes them the most rate-sensitive private holdings there are.

questions.description: A fund takes 25-35% stakes in software businesses with $30-80m of revenue growing 40%+ a year, mostly unprofitable. It uses no fund-level or deal-level leverage, holds two board seats per company, negotiates liquidation preferences, and expects exits via trade sale or IPO in four to six years.
choices: Growth equity
Buyout
Venture capital
Private credit
rationales: Correct. Minority stakes, no leverage, revenue already substantial and growing fast, negotiated protections and a medium-term exit horizon is growth equity precisely.
Buyout takes control, uses substantial leverage, and targets cash-generative businesses. None of those apply here.
Venture invests earlier, at smaller revenue or pre-revenue, in much smaller stakes across many more companies, expecting most to fail.
Private credit lends rather than taking equity stakes, and would not hold board seats or liquidation preferences of this kind.
questions.explanation: The distinguishing combination is substantial existing revenue with rapid growth, minority position, and no leverage. Revenue at that scale rules out venture; the absence of control and debt rules out buyout.

questions.stem: Why do subsequent financing rounds at flat or lower valuations matter more than a manager's current marks?
choices: Because they are audited and marks are not
Because they are third-party price signals that appear well before a manager adjusts their own valuation
Because a down round automatically triggers a write-off
Because they determine the fund's management fee
rationales: Neither is audited in the sense implied. The relevant difference is that one involves a third party committing money.

Correct. A new investor pricing the company is real evidence, and it typically precedes any change in the existing holder's mark. It is one of the few genuinely independent signals available in a private portfolio.
A down round reduces value but does not require a write-off. Managers often mark down partially or not at all.
Fees are usually charged on commitments or invested capital, not on individual round valuations.
questions.explanation: In a portfolio where nearly every number is the manager's own opinion, a third party committing capital at a stated price is a rare piece of external evidence. Tracking round-over-round valuations across a portfolio is one of the most useful monitoring habits available.
